=== CALL C0278 ===
Joanne: Hiya! Oh, hello, can you hear me alright? I'm never sure with these things.
Lee: Yeah, loud and clear. Alright?
Joanne: Yes, good thanks! I'm Joanne, I'm in Taunton. Did you manage that puzzle thing? I was all fingers and thumbs.
Lee: Lee. Bridgwater. Puzzle was alright, last couple did my head in a bit though.
Joanne: Bridgwater! Oh, I was born in Bridgwater, me. My dad worked out at Hinkley for years, the old station, you know.
Lee: Yeah? Don't get me started on Hinkley, mate. Rent on my place has gone up twice in two years 'cos of all the workers coming in. Landlord knows he can get it, do you know what I mean? Though to be fair a couple of the lads I went school with are on proper money out there.
Joanne: Oh, it's sort of swings and roundabouts, isn't it. And the traffic on the M5 by you, honestly, I sat there forty minutes last week.
Lee: Junction twenty-three's a joke. What d'you do then?
Joanne: Erm, well, nothing at the moment really, which sounds awful. I was a veterinary nurse for over twenty years, head nurse at the end, but my back went and the shifts were killing me, so I stopped about three years ago. I help out at a cat rescue now, few hours a week. Sorry, that's a lot!
Lee: Nah, you're alright. What's up with your back then?
Joanne: Lower back, it's been on and off for years. Lifting Labradors onto tables doesn't help, you know!
Lee: Slipped disc, me. Four years back. Used to do five-a-side, can't now. Some mornings I can barely get out the van.
Joanne: Oh, you poor thing. What is it you do?
Lee: Mechanic. Independent garage out on the industrial estate, MOTs and that. Lot of bending under bonnets, so, yeah.
Joanne: Oh gosh, that's not ideal with a back. Do they look after you there?
Lee: Look after me? Boss pays sod all for what we do. I'm the one finding the faults the main dealers can't, and he's sat in his office. I'll do my own thing in a couple of years, mobile mechanic, then I don't answer to no one.
Joanne: Well, good for you. You'd have people queuing up, I bet. People are always wanting someone they trust with their car.
Lee: That's it. Half the time customers have been fobbed off somewhere else before they get to me.
Joanne: My Martin's hopeless with ours. He's a surveyor, he can tell you everything about a damp wall but not where the oil goes!
Lee: Ha. Classic.
Joanne: Have you got any pets? Sorry, I always ask, it's the nurse in me.
Lee: Diesel. Staffie cross. He's sat here now actually. Chewed the remote again this morning.
Joanne: Oh, bless him! They do love a remote, I think it smells of your hands, that's the thing, it's comforting. Mine's Biscuit, Border terrier, he's an old grump. Won't go out if it's raining, just stands on the doorstep looking at me like it's my fault.
Lee: Diesel'd go out in a hurricane. Take him along the river most nights.
Joanne: Do you go up the Quantocks? I love it up there when my back lets me.
Lee: Sometimes weekends, yeah. Mostly it's Carnival I'm counting down to though. November.
Joanne: Oh, Bridgwater Carnival! I haven't been in years, we used to go every year as kids. Are you in it?
Lee: Know a few in one of the carts. I help out with the generators and the lights and that. Proper mental how big they are now, thousands of bulbs.
Joanne: Oh, that's lovely though, isn't it? That's proper community, that is. I might have to drag Martin along.
Lee: You should. Get there early, mind, parking's a nightmare.
Joanne: I'll remember that! Sorry, I've been waffling on, haven't I?
Lee: Nah. Better than sitting here in silence.
Joanne: That's true! Oh, I think we've only got a minute left.

=== CALL C0279 ===
Agnieszka: Hello! Hi, sorry, can you hear me? I think it's working.
Helen: Yes, I can hear you. Hello.
Agnieszka: Oh, good. I'm Agnieszka, I'm in Basingstoke. Sorry, it's a long name, people just say Aga sometimes.
Helen: I'm Helen. Otley, near Leeds.
Agnieszka: Ah, Yorkshire! Did you find the puzzle okay? I was so worried I was doing it wrong, I checked the instructions about three times.
Helen: Erm, it was alright. The last one took me a while. I think I overthought it.
Agnieszka: Me too, exactly the same! So, what do you do, if you don't mind me asking?
Helen: I'm an archivist. At a university library in Leeds, special collections. Three days a week.
Agnieszka: Oh, that's interesting. So like old documents, letters?
Helen: Yes, mostly. Letters, diaries, estate papers. I catalogue them so people can actually find what's there. And I supervise the reading room some days. It's quiet work, which suits me, if that makes sense.
Agnieszka: It makes total sense. I'm executive assistant to a finance director, sorry, Chief Financial Officer, at insurance company. So his diary, board papers, travel. Not so quiet! But I like it. I've been with him six years now, I know exactly how he wants everything.
Helen: Six years is a long time with one person. You must know his handwriting by now.
Agnieszka: Oh, his handwriting is terrible! Honestly, I'm the only one in office who can read it. People bring me his notes like I'm translator.
Helen: That's half my job, really. Seventeenth-century handwriting is probably not so different from a finance director's.
Agnieszka: Ha, maybe! Do you have family up there?
Helen: My daughter, Isla. She's nine. And my mum's nearby, she helps with the school pick-up.
Agnieszka: Oh, my daughter is nine as well! Zosia. Year Four?
Helen: Year Four, yes.
Agnieszka: That's so funny. She has swimming on Thursdays and Polish school on Saturdays, so I'm like a taxi, you know?
Helen: Polish school, that's good. Does she like it?
Agnieszka: Mostly. Sometimes she complains. But I want her to talk properly with my parents, they're in Rzeszów, they don't speak much English. I fly back twice a year but, erm, they're getting older, so.
Helen: Is it far? From the airport, I mean.
Agnieszka: Not bad, there's a flight from Luton straight to Rzeszów. Two hours. I'm always at airport much too early, Tomasz, my husband, he laughs at me.
Helen: I'd be the same. I like knowing where I'm meant to be.
Agnieszka: Yes! Everything in one plastic folder, passports, everything.
Helen: That's not daft. I lost a boarding pass in Norway once, years ago. Never again.
Agnieszka: Norway! Was it beautiful?
Helen: It was. The Lofoten Islands. Before Isla. I'd like to take her one day, when she's old enough to walk properly without moaning.
Agnieszka: Oh, that sounds lovely. We usually do Croatia or Portugal, with another Polish family. Very easy, kids play, we sit.
Helen: That sounds quite relaxing, actually.
Agnieszka: It is. Sorry, I'm talking a lot, is that okay?
Helen: It's fine. I'm not much of a talker, so it helps.
Agnieszka: Okay, good! I think we have maybe one minute?

calls.C0278:

Annelies: The ferry is better for that. You get on in the evening, have a meal, sleep, and you wake up in Rotterdam.

Annelies: Most things are nicer than Luton.
Agnieszka: Ha! True. Is your family still there?
Annelies: My sister, in Utrecht. And my mother. She's, erm, she's not so well now. It's hard being far away.
Agnieszka: Yes. My parents also, they're getting older. I'm always thinking, if something happens, I'm two hours away, plus airport. Sorry, that's sad thing to talk about.
Annelies: No, it's alright. It's nice to talk to someone who understands it.
Agnieszka: Yes. Okay, something happier. Do you garden? I saw a bird feeder.
Annelies: A little. Vegetables in the back. And a robin has started coming to the feeder, which I'm very chuffed about.
Agnieszka: Oh, lovely. My hanging baskets all died in the heatwave. All of them.
Annelies: Mine too, actually. I forgot to water them for one weekend.
Agnieszka: One weekend, that's all it takes!
Annelies: I think we're almost at time.
calls.C0284:
Joanne: Hiya! Oh, hello, can you hear me alright?
Shahida: Yes. Hello.
Joanne: I'm Joanne, I'm in Taunton, down in Somerset. That's three of these I've done now, I'm getting the hang of it!
Shahida: Shahida. Ilford. Last one for me also.
Joanne: Oh, lovely. Have the others been nice? I've had a mechanic and an archivist, would you believe. Sorry, I'm already waffling!
Shahida: The mechanic, yes, I had him also. He doesn't eat properly, that boy.
Joanne: Ha! Oh, I did wonder. Energy drinks and pasties, I bet. My son's the same, he's twenty-two, lives in Bristol, comes home weekends with a bag of washing.
Shahida: That photo in your kitchen, on the window, those are your children? I thought grandchildren.
Joanne: Oh, bless you, no, that's Callum and Ellie! Although some days I feel old enough to be a nan. Have you got grandchildren?
Shahida: Five. Two I look after, my elder son's. Two days a week I pick up from school, I give them dinner, homework, then he comes. Seven and five. The little one, very clever, very naughty.
Joanne: Oh, they're the best ones, the naughty clever ones. What do you cook them?
Shahida: Proper food. Daal, roti, chicken. I make the roti fresh every day. Forty years I'm making same food, nobody complains.
Joanne: Well, if it's not broke! I'm a shepherd's pie and roast sort of cook, and curries from a jar, but I jazz them up, you know, bit of extra garlic. You'd probably be horrified.
Shahida: Jar curry, hm. It's ok. Everybody is busy.
Joanne: That's very diplomatic of you! What did you used to do? Before, I mean, if you did work?
Shahida: Ladies' clothing shop, Green Street. Suits, fabric. Fifteen years. I stopped at sixty, my knees.
Joanne: Oh, knees and backs, honestly, the whole lot of us are falling apart. I was a vet nurse twenty years and my back finished me off. I do a bit at a cat rescue now, unpaid, but I'd love to find something part-time, sitting down. I just worry I'm out of the loop now, you know, three years off, everything's on computers. Sorry, does that make sense?
Shahida: You can learn computer. I did computer course at the library, ten years ago, I was nearly sixty. Now I do surveys, WhatsApp, everything.
Joanne: Oh, that's really encouraging, actually.
Shahida: Twenty years nurse, you know animals, you know people. Somebody will take you. Don't say "only" this, "only" that.
Joanne: Oh, gosh. Thank you. That's, erm, that's just what I needed to hear really.
Shahida: Hm. That's it.
Joanne: Do you sew? Sorry, I'm guessing, it's the fabric shop.
Shahida: Yes, all the family, I do alterations. Weddings, I take in, take out. They don't pay me, of course.
Joanne: Same as my traybakes for church! Nobody ever pays for a traybake.
Shahida: You have nice house, your kitchen. Very clean.
Joanne: Oh, it's not always, I'd tidied for the camera!
Shahida: Acha. I think time is finishing now.
calls.C0285:
Annelies: Hello. Can you hear me?
Helen: Yes. Hello. I'm Helen.
Annelies: Annelies. I'm in Sheffield.
Helen: Otley. So not too far, really.
Annelies: No. Over the moors. Erm, I think I recognise your bookcase from the photograph.
Helen: It's hard to miss. I keep saying I'll sort it out.
Annelies: You stack them sideways, I noticed. I do that too when the shelf is full. My husband says it looks like a library that's given up.
Helen: That's quite accurate. I work in an archive, so I've no excuse.
Annelies: Oh, an archive. Which one?
Helen: Special collections, at a university in Leeds. Letters, diaries, mill records. I'm cataloguing a family's letters at the moment. Nineteenth century, mostly the women writing to each other. It's very slow work but I like it. You get to know their handwriting, and then you sort of get to know them.
Annelies: That sounds lovely. I'm at the university here, but in the office side. Executive assistant to a head of faculty. Very little handwriting, a lot of committee papers.
Helen: Less romantic.
Annelies: Much less. What are you reading at the moment, then? For yourself, I mean.
Helen: Erm, a Norwegian novel. I'm halfway through and I'm still not sure if I like it. Everybody stares at the sea a lot.
Annelies: That's often the way with them. My book group is reading a Japanese one this month. There are five of us. Two loved it, two hated it, and I'm in the middle.
Helen: Which one?
Annelies: About a woman who works in a convenience store. I can't remember the author, sorry.
Helen: Oh, I know it. I liked that one. I thought she was the only sensible person in it.
Annelies: Yes, I thought that too, actually. I'll tell the group.
Helen: Do you walk? You've got the look of someone who walks. Sorry, that's an odd thing to say.
Annelies: No, it's true. The Peak District, most weekends, with Graham. I take a small notebook and do watercolour sketches. Very bad ones.
Helen: I draw plants. Foxgloves, hedgerow things. Pencil, then a bit of watercolour.
Annelies: Oh, the foxglove behind you. That's yours?
Helen: It is, yes.
Annelies: It's not bad at all. It's very good.
Helen: Thank you. I don't show people usually.
Annelies: No, I don't either. Graham has started baking sourdough. The whole kitchen is covered in flour.
Helen: I've had a starter going three years. It didn't rise at the weekend, though. I think it's sulking.
Annelies: I'll tell him they sulk. He'll be relieved it's not him.
Helen: It's usually the weather. Or the flour. Never the baker.
Annelies: That's what I'll say, then. Erm, I think we're nearly out of time.
Helen: Yes. It's been nice. Quiet, in a good way.
calls.C0286:
Agnieszka: Hello! Hi, can you hear me?
Lee: Yeah. Alright?
Agnieszka: Yes, good, thank you. I'm Agnieszka, in Basingstoke.
Lee: Lee. Bridgwater.
Agnieszka: Somerset, yes? Is it near Taunton? I think I spoke to... no, sorry, that was someone else.
Lee: Up the road from Taunton, yeah. You'll have had Joanne, maybe. Nice woman.
Agnieszka: No, not yet, but she looked very nice in the photo. What do you do?
Lee: Mechanic. Independent garage. You in an office?
Agnieszka: Yes, executive assistant, for a finance director at insurance company. Very boring for you, probably.
Lee: Didn't say that. Thought you looked like accounts or summat.
Agnieszka: Close! I do some budget things. My husband, Tomasz, he's maintenance engineer, distribution centre. He fixes everything at home also. Our car, it's making a noise at the moment, like a sort of, erm, clunk, when we go over speed bumps.
Lee: Front or back?
Agnieszka: Front, I think. Front side, the left.
Lee: Sounds like a drop link or an anti-roll bar bush, nine times out of ten. Cheap part. If a garage tells you it's the whole strut, get a second opinion. People get fobbed off with that all the time, do you know what I mean? They see someone who don't know cars and they add two hundred quid.
Agnieszka: Oh, that's so useful, thank you. I will tell Tomasz. He says it's nothing, but I worry.
Lee: Probably is nothing. Don't leave it forever, mind.
Agnieszka: What do you drive yourself?
Lee: Golf GTI, twenty-twelve. Done a few bits to it. Remap, exhaust, wheels. Still paying it off, mind.
Agnieszka: Oh, very fast, then.
Lee: Fast enough. Not that you can go fast anywhere, M5's a car park half the time.
Agnieszka: For us it's the Ringway in the morning. Every day, same queue, same roundabout. I listen to Polish radio and I just, you know, breathe.
Lee: Polish, yeah? How long you been over?
Agnieszka: Since 2007. I was twenty-three. My parents are still in Rzeszów, I fly twice a year.
Lee: Fair play. Don't think I could do that, I've never been further than Lanzarote. All my lot's within fifteen mile.
Agnieszka: That's nice, having everybody close. Sometimes I'm jealous of that, honestly.
Lee: Yeah, can be a bit much, Sunday dinner at my mum's every week. Still. Wouldn't swap it.
Agnieszka: No. Sorry, I'm asking so many questions, is that okay?
Lee: You're alright. Better than the last one, she was asking what I eat.
Agnieszka: Oh no! I won't ask that, I promise.
Lee: Cheers. Drop link, remember. Tell your fella.
Agnieszka: Drop link. I'm writing it down now. I think we have one minute.
calls.C0287:
Joanne: Hiya! Oh, it's you! I said when I saw your photo, she looks a lot like me. Is that a terrible thing to say?
Annelies: No, not at all. I thought something similar, actually. The cardigan, the kitchen.
Joanne: Ha! Uniform of women our age, isn't it. I'm Joanne, Taunton.
Annelies: Annelies. Sheffield.
Joanne: Oh, lovely. Have you had a nice time with these? I've been chatting away to everyone, poor things.
Annelies: Yes, they've been nice. I spoke to Helen just now, the archivist. We talked about books mostly.
Joanne: Oh, she's lovely, isn't she? Quiet, but she's got a proper dry sense of humour once you get her going. She let me count ABBA as a hymn.
Annelies: She was very kind about my watercolours. Which they don't deserve.
Joanne: Oh, I bet they're better than you say. You've got the bird feeder, haven't you, I saw it in your window. Get much on it?
Annelies: A robin, lately. He comes every morning about half seven, while I'm having my tea. Sorry, my cup of tea, I mean, not my meal. I've been in Yorkshire too long.
Joanne: No, I'm the same, I say tea and dinner and nobody knows what I'm on about. Where are you from originally?
Annelies: The Netherlands. Amersfoort. More than thirty years ago now.
Joanne: Gosh. Do you still have family over there?
Annelies: My sister. And my mother. She's in the early stages of dementia, erm, so I go over when I can. It's not easy, being on the ferry every time something happens.
Joanne: Oh, love. My mum's starting with it too. Little things, you know, she put the kettle in the fridge last month and laughed it off, but I could see she was frightened. And I'm only forty minutes away and I still feel like I'm not doing enough. So goodness knows how you manage it from another country.
Annelies: Badly, some weeks. I feel guilty a lot. My sister does most of it.
Joanne: I don't think you should feel guilty. You're ringing, you're going over. That's not nothing. Sorry, I don't mean to tell you how to feel.
Annelies: No, it's kind. Thank you. It's nice to hear it from someone who knows.
Joanne: Do you go to church at all? Sorry, that's a nosy one. It's just it helps me, sort of, sitting there.
Annelies: Yes, most Sundays. I don't say much about it. But I think it helps me too.
Joanne: Same. I'm on the flower rota, which is mostly an excuse for coffee and gossip, if I'm honest.
Annelies: I bake for ours. A Dutch apple cake. It disappears very quickly.
Joanne: Oh, I'd love that recipe! I do traybakes. Lemon drizzle, millionaire's shortbread. I take them to choir and all.
Annelies: You sing?
Joanne: Community choir. Pop, musicals. Nothing like the proper stuff.
Annelies: I listen to choral music on Radio 3. I cry at it, which is embarrassing.
Joanne: Oh, I cry at Strictly results, so you're doing better than me!
Annelies: I think we're nearly finished. It went fast.
Joanne: It did. You take care of yourself, won't you?
calls.C0288:
Agnieszka: Hello! Hi, can you hear me okay?
Shahida: Yes. I thought last one was finished, then another one comes.
Agnieszka: Oh, sorry! I think it's four rounds. I'm Agnieszka, I'm in Basingstoke.
Shahida: Shahida. Ilford.
Agnieszka: Nice to meet you. How has it been, the calls?
Shahida: Ok. Everybody very polite. The mechanic, he doesn't eat properly.
Agnieszka: Oh, Lee! He helped me with my car, actually. A noise in the front. He said it's a drop link, I wrote it down.
Shahida: Good. Free advice, that's the best kind.
Agnieszka: Exactly! Normally the garage, they charge you just to look.
Shahida: Everything costs now. You do your shopping where?
Agnieszka: Aldi, mostly. And there is Polish shop on the high street, for bread, sausage, things from home. But they keep running out of the good bread, it's so annoying.
Shahida: New Lidl near me, very cheap. Fruit, veg, good price. Meat I don't buy there, only from my butcher.
Agnieszka: Yes, I understand, you have your butcher you trust. My mum is the same in Rzeszów, thirty years the same man.
Shahida: Correct. Same man, he knows me, he doesn't give me rubbish.
Agnieszka: Do you cook every day?
Shahida: Every day. Roti fresh. Daal, karahi. My grandchildren, two days a week, I feed them.
Agnieszka: Oh, that's lovely. I have a daughter, Zosia, she's nine. I cook most evenings, but simple. Pasta bake, soup. When my mum visits, we make pierogi together, hundreds, and I freeze them.
Shahida: Pierogi, what is it?
Agnieszka: Sort of dumplings. Dough, and inside potato and cheese, or cabbage, or meat. You boil them, then fry with onion.
Shahida: Like samosa, but boiled. Ok. Freezing is clever. I also freeze, parathas, keema, ready for the week.
Agnieszka: Yes! Then on a busy day, you have something proper, you know?
Shahida: Better than takeaway. You live in house or flat?
Agnieszka: House, a semi. We bought in 2015, on a newer estate. Still mortgage, of course.
Shahida: We finished ours long time ago. Own outright. My husband wanted new car, I said no, house first.
Agnieszka: That's very wise. That's what I want also, security. More than anything, really, after Brexit and everything. Sorry, that's a big topic.
Shahida: Hm. People say things. You have your house, your job, your passport. Then they can say what they like.
Agnieszka: Yes. That's true. I got citizenship in 2019, for that reason. Peace of mind.
Shahida: Good. Paper is important. That's it.
Agnieszka: I bake also, cheesecake, for work. Do you bake?
Shahida: No. Diabetes. Doctor says no sugar, so I don't make sweet things now. Only for Eid.
Agnieszka: Oh, sorry. Only for Eid is fair, I think.
Shahida: Acha. Time is finishing, I think.
calls.C0289:
Joanne: Hiya! Oh, finally, it's you! I've been hoping I'd get you. Can you hear me alright?
Agnieszka: Yes! Hello! I was hoping also, honestly. I saw your photo at the beginning and I thought, she looks so friendly.
Joanne: Oh, stop it, you'll set me off! I'm Joanne, Taunton.
Agnieszka: Agnieszka, Basingstoke. Lee said you were nice, actually. He told me about his drop links.
Joanne: Ha! Did he fix your car over the video? He's a good lad, that one, bit grumpy about his boss, mind.
Agnieszka: He diagnosed it in thirty seconds. I wrote it down for my husband.
Joanne: Oh, that's brilliant. So what do you do, then? I'm guessing something organised, with that calendar behind you.
Agnieszka: Executive assistant, for a CFO at insurance company. Diary, board papers, travel, all of it. I check everything three times, sorry, four times sometimes.
Joanne: Oh, I'd be the same. I used to do the rota at the practice, I was head vet nurse before my back went, and I'd lie awake thinking, have I put two people on the Saturday? Erm, I'm not working now, three years, I just help at a cat rescue. And I keep thinking about a little part-time job, reception or something, but then I think, oh, they won't want me, I'm out of the loop. Sorry, I've said that to about four people today!
Agnieszka: But you should go for it! You know animals, you know people. And reception, honestly, it's mostly being calm when someone is panicking. That's half my job too.
Joanne: That's what Shahida said! Well, sort of, she was a bit sterner about it.
Agnieszka: Ha, yes, she's very direct. I liked her.
Joanne: Oh, me too, in the end. Have you got children?
Agnieszka: One, Zosia, she's nine. Swimming Thursdays, Polish school Saturdays.
Joanne: Oh, busy girl. Mine are grown up now, twenty-two and nineteen. Ellie's at uni in Cardiff and I worry about her constantly, living in a city, walking home at night, all that. She rings when she wants money and I'm just relieved she's alive!
Agnieszka: I think I will be the same. Already I worry and she's only nine.
Joanne: Oh, it doesn't stop, love. Do you do anything for yourself?
Agnieszka: Pilates, Tuesday evenings, with a friend from work. And walking at lunchtime.
Joanne: No! I do Pilates on a Tuesday! Mornings, though. I'm always shattered after.
Agnieszka: Me too, and it's only stretching, how is it so tiring?
Joanne: I know! And musicals? You look like a musicals person.
Agnieszka: Oh yes. Les Misérables, twice in London. I cried both times, the whole second half.
Joanne: Oh, "Bring Him Home", I'm gone every time. We're doing ABBA at choir, not quite the same.
Agnieszka: ABBA is happy crying, at least.
Joanne: That's true! Oh, and my hanging baskets haven't taken this year, would you believe.
Agnieszka: Mine died in the heatwave! Everybody's baskets are dead today, I think.
Joanne: It's a national tragedy. Oh, we must be nearly out of time.
Agnieszka: I think so. It was so nice to talk, really.
calls.C0290:
Shahida: Hello. Another one.
Helen: Hello. Yes, I think this is the last. I'm Helen.
Shahida: Shahida. Ilford. Five calls, I didn't know it is five.
Helen: Nor did I, to be honest. I'm in Otley, near Leeds.
Shahida: You have many books. In your picture. You are teacher?
Helen: Erm, no, not quite. Archivist. I look after old papers at a university library. Letters, diaries.
Shahida: Old letters. People pay for this?
Helen: Not very much. But yes. Someone has to make sure they don't get thrown away. Otherwise in fifty years nobody knows what happened.
Shahida: Hm. My mother's letters from Lahore, I still have them. In a box, in the wardrobe.
Helen: Do you? I'd keep them dry. And not in plastic, if you can help it, it makes them sweat.
Shahida: Ok. I didn't know. My daughter says throw old things, I say no.
Helen: I'm on your side there.
Shahida: You have children?
Helen: A daughter, Isla. She's nine.
Shahida: Husband?
Helen: No. We weren't married. Her dad's in Bradford, she goes to him every other weekend. It works, mostly. And my mum helps, she does the Tuesday pick-up.
Shahida: Good. Grandmother is important. I do my son's children, two days. Seven and five. I give them dinner, I check homework. Their mother is busy.
Helen: My mum would say the same about me, probably.
Shahida: Your mum is right. Mothers are usually right.
Helen: She wants to get a dog at the moment. She's seventy. I've told her it'll be me walking it.
Shahida: Of course it will be you. My husband wanted a dog once. I said who cleans? He went quiet.
Helen: That's a good question to ask, actually. I might borrow it.
Shahida: Borrow, ok. What you eat for dinner, with your daughter?
Helen: Erm, simple things. Lentil soup, pasta. I'm usually too tired by six to do much. I bake bread at the weekend, though.
Shahida: Lentils is good. Daal is lentils. Put cumin, garlic, little chilli for you, not too much for child.
Helen: I'll try that. Isla likes things plain, so it'll be a negotiation.
Shahida: Children must eat what you make. That's it.
Helen: You'd do well in our house.
Shahida: Everybody says. You walk a lot? You look thin.
Helen: I walk up the Chevin most Sundays, the hill by the town. Early, before anyone's about.
Shahida: Alone? Be careful.
Helen: I will. There's mostly just a heron and the odd dog walker.
Shahida: Acha. I think now time is finishing. Bas.
Helen: Yes. Thank you, it was nice to talk.

C0279.line_text: Mostly. Sometimes she complains. But I want her to talk properly with my parents, they're in Rzeszów, they don't speak much English. I fly back twice a year but, erm, they're getting older, so.
C0279.what: As she says 'they're getting older', her smile drops and she looks away to her left towards the window for two or three seconds, pressing her lips together, then looks back at the camera before 'so'.
